expect:
Arguments in support:
• Guru Granth Sahib 349 explicitly condemns caste — 'born from same clay' — placing equality at the heart of revealed teaching.
• Practical institutions (langar, sangat, sewa) express equality in everyday Sikh life, making it more than abstract doctrine.
• Guru Gobind Singh's Khalsa abolished caste-based names, giving equality structural expression in Sikh identity.
• Non-religious view: humanist thinkers argue equality is the foundation of human dignity independently of any religious framework.
Arguments against:
• The authority of the Guru Granth Sahib as living Guru could be considered more fundamental — without this source of authority, equality teachings lose their divine grounding.
• Belief in one God (Waheguru) and the goal of mukti (union with God) might be argued as the theological foundation that makes all other teachings, including equality, possible.
• The Khalsa's five commitments (Five Ks) could be seen as the defining Sikh teaching because they involve active, visible commitment, not just belief.
Conclusion: A justified personal judgement weighing which teaching is most fundamental.
Mastering: Sustained two-sided argument with named sources, non-religious view included, clear justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides developed, at least one source, conclusion present.
Developing: One side stronger than other, limited sources.
Emerging: One-sided or no conclusion.
